title: What To Do With Old Rakhis: Traditional Beliefs and Eco-Friendly Options
excerpt: Hindu tradition advises against throwing rakhis in the trash. Here is when to remove the sacred thread, how to dispose of it respectfully, and sustainable alternatives gaining ground.
body:
• Traditional Hindu belief holds that rakhis should never be thrown in the garbage — proper disposal includes immersion in flowing water, tying to a sacred tree, or burying near a plant
  • Multiple traditions govern when to remove the rakhi: after 15-16 days, on Janmashtami, or as late as Dussehra, depending on regional custom
  • An estimated 620 million rakhis end up in landfills annually in India, many made from plastic, synthetic thread, and non-biodegradable glitter
  • Eco-friendly alternatives — seed rakhis, cotton-thread rakhis, and plantable designs — are gaining popularity as sustainable options

As Raksha Bandhan approaches, millions of sisters will tie rakhis on their brothers' wrists, renewing a bond rooted in centuries of Hindu tradition. But a question that comes up every year — and one many families handle differently — is what to do with the rakhi afterward. Should it stay on the wrist? When should it come off? And what is the right way to part with it?

The answers vary by region, family practice, and scriptural interpretation, but one thing is consistent across traditions: throwing a rakhi in the dustbin is considered disrespectful and inauspicious.

When To Remove the Rakhi

In Sanatan tradition, the rakhi is not merely decorative — it is regarded as a protective thread that shields the brother from negative energies. Removing it too quickly is considered inauspicious.

Several traditions govern the timing:

The 15-day rule: Many families follow the practice of keeping the rakhi tied from Purnima (the full moon day of Raksha Bandhan) through the next 15 days. This period is believed to strengthen the sibling bond and the protective power of the thread.

Until Janmashtami: In some communities, the rakhi stays on the wrist until Janmashtami (Lord Krishna's birthday), which typically falls about a week after Raksha Bandhan. After Janmashtami, the rakhi is removed and immersed in flowing water or placed under a sacred tree.

The 16-day rule: According to Panchang-based astrology, keeping the rakhi for 16 days and immersing it in flowing water on the 16th day is believed to bring longevity, success, and prosperity to the brother.

Until Dussehra: The most conservative practice, observed in parts of North India, holds that the rakhi should remain on the wrist until Vijayadashami (Dussehra), the festival celebrating good over evil. The rakhi is believed to serve as a protective shield throughout this period.

One month (Sawan to Bhadra Purnima): Some shastras (ancient scriptures) advise keeping the rakhi for a full month, from Sawan Purnima to Bhadra Purnima.

The Right Way To Dispose of a Rakhi

Across all traditions, the rakhi is treated as a sacred object that deserves respectful disposal — similar to how puja materials are handled after worship.

Water immersion (visarjan): The most common method. The rakhi is immersed in a river, pond, or any clean flowing water body. If no natural water source is accessible, it can be placed in a bowl of clean water in the puja room, and the water later poured at the base of a tree.

Tying to a sacred tree: The rakhi can be tied to a Tulsi (holy basil) plant, Peepal tree, or Neem tree — all considered sacred in Hindu tradition. This symbolizes continued protection and positivity.

Burying near a plant: Digging a small hole and burying the rakhi near a plant in the garden or a pot ensures the thread returns to the earth.

"It is never appropriate to ignore and throw away the Rakhi. This is a sacred thread. After removing it, it is best to immerse it in a river or pond, as it is believed that it takes away all the troubles and negative energy."

— Traditional guidance on rakhi disposal

If the rakhi breaks early: Tradition advises wrapping the broken rakhi in a red or yellow cloth and either immersing it in water or offering it at a sacred site on the next Purnima day.

Burning the rakhi or tossing it in the garbage is strongly discouraged — it is viewed as dishonoring the sacred bond the thread represents.

The Environmental Angle

Beyond tradition, there is a growing practical reason to rethink rakhi disposal. According to estimates from sustainable gifting platforms, around 620 million rakhis end up in Indian landfills every year. Many modern rakhis are made from plastic, synthetic thread, metallic foil, and non-biodegradable glitter that can sit in landfills for centuries and leach toxic dyes into soil and water.

This has fueled a movement toward eco-friendly alternatives. Seed rakhis — made from natural clay embedded with basil, ashwagandha, or flower seeds — can be planted after use. Cotton and jute thread rakhis decompose naturally. Some organizations make rakhis from cow dung mixed with turmeric and sandalwood, which can be composted. Others design rakhis as reusable bracelets or jewelry.

For the Diaspora

For Indian families abroad, respectful rakhi disposal can be adapted to local settings. Immersion works in any clean water body. Burying near a houseplant or garden is simple. Tying to a backyard tree, while not a Tulsi or Peepal, still honors the spirit of the tradition. What matters, across all interpretations, is treating the rakhi as more than a disposable accessory — it is a thread that carried a prayer.
